case_name: Ranjitham and another v Basavaraj and another
respondent:
Basavaraj and another

CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.1453 OF 2005 WITH CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.1700 OF 2005
(Non-Reportable)
The Judgment was delivered by : Ranjana Prakash Desai, J.

facts: These two appeals, by special leave, can be disposed of by a common judgment as they challenge the judgment and order dated 14/3/2005 passed by the Madras High Court in Criminal Appeal No.130 of 1997 filed by Swami Kannu, Basavaraj, Kumaran, Kanagaraj and Gnanapazham (original accused 1 to 5 respectively) who are hereinafter referred to as 'A1' to 'A5' respectively for convenience.
In Sessions Case No.151 of 1993, A1 to A5 were charged for offence punishable under Section 147 of the IPC.
The case of the prosecution needs to be narrated in brief.
On 11/11/1992 at about 7.30 p.m., PW-1 Pandurangan, PW-4 Jabbar and one Nanjappan were sitting near a bus stop at Dharmapuri.
A2 refused to pay the amount and made some disparaging remarks about the deceased.
The relations between the accused and the deceased were strained.
On 11/11/1992 the situation in Madhikonpalayam village was tense.
issues: Whether A2 attacked the deceased in exercise of his right of private defence?
Whether the trial court's findings are perverse?
petitioner_arguments: The High Court was wrong in accepting the argument that A2 attacked the deceased in exercise of his right of private defence.
It is the accused who were the aggressors and, therefore, plea of private defence could not have been raised by them.
There is cogent and adequate evidence of eye-witnesses which has been overlooked.
respondent_arguments: Substantial part of the prosecution story is disbelieved by the trial court.
This being an appeal against order of acquittal, this Court should be slow in disturbing the order of acquittal.
The evidence on record clearly establishes the theory of right of private defence and, hence, the appeals deserve to be dismissed.
court_reasoning: Unless it appears to us that the impugned judgment is perverse, we cannot interfere with it.

If two views are possible on appreciating the evidence and if the view taken by the acquitting court is a reasonably possible view we cannot substitute it by the other view just because it appears to us to be a possible view.
holding: The appeals deserve to be dismissed.
